text.content:
Essence is a tabletop game about sharp, tactical combat and roleplay that stays entirely in your hands. When a fight breaks out, you'll manage dice pools, positioning, and a hand of cards that spell out exactly what your character can do. Outside of combat, the rules step back and your table drives the story.

This guide covers how to actually play a session from inside Foundry — your character sheet, rolling dice, and running combat through the tools this system gives you. For the full rules themselves, see the Combat Styles Reference journal and the Essence rulebook (v0.6).

Three Domains, No Classes

Every character is built from three domains — Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). There's no class to pick. Your Attributes, Combat Styles, Species, Heritage, Distinction, and equipment combine into a character that's genuinely yours — two people who both invest in the same Combat Style can still play completely differently.

Where to Start

New to the sheet? Read Your Character Sheet next, then Combat once you're ready to fight. Everything else can wait until it comes up at the table.

Open your character from the Actors sidebar tab. Don't have one yet? Click Create Character, then open the wand icon in the sheet's header to launch the Character Creation Wizard — it walks you through Attributes, Career, Skills and Languages, Species/Heritage/Distinction, Combat Styles, cards and starting Equipment, and records your starting Advancement Points at the end.

Your sheet is split into tabs: Core (Attributes, Resources, Wounds, Death Track), Combat (Action/Reaction Cards and your Combat Style Specialties), Equipment (Inventory, Temporary, Armory), Non-Combat (Skills, Key Aspects, Reach and Influence, Connections), and Biography. Everything you need in a given moment lives on the relevant tab.

Your character belongs to a Team: a Team actor holds the group's Team Tier and record. Link to it from the Non-Combat tab. Team Tier governs which equipment Components are within ordinary access; it is not a rating of you or of your enemies.

Your 9 Attributes sit inside the three domains: Physical (Might, Grace, Vigor), Mental (Intellect, Acuity, Resolve), and Spiritual (Presence, Adaptability, Anima). Each domain also has a Resource you spend to act (Stamina, Focus, Mana) and a Defense others roll against to hit you (Fortitude, Composure, Harmony). A Defense is 2 plus the two lowest Attributes of its domain and never falls below 0.

Each domain covers three Combat Styles as well. Five of the nine — Gestalt, Magecraft, Psionics, Ritualism, and Calling — are gated: you need the matching Distinction before you can raise them above 0. Your sheet greys these out until you qualify. For the Style tied to your Distinction, your Expertise limit is one higher than the Style's Rank.

Your base Action and Reaction Pools are 6 dice each, plus any explicit pool increase. Advancement is measured in Advancement Points (shown as Level on the sheet) spent through the Skill Tree.

Each Attribute also does something outside its dice pools. The sheet shows a one-line reminder under each Attribute; the rules in brief:

  • Might — carry 50 lb of exceptional cargo per point beyond personal equipment, with actual support and hands. Hauling doubles Movement cost.
  • Grace — running horizontal jump up to Grace units, with 2 units of run-up and a suitable landing.
  • Vigor — hold breath or sustain extreme effort for Vigor minutes (6 × Vigor Rounds) before the hazard procedure. Fatigued is the default strain Condition.
  • Intellect — 1 Non-Combat Skill Point per permanent point (creation maximum Rank 2, advancement maximum Rank 5).
  • Acuity — one primary language plus Acuity additional languages. Record them on the Non-Combat tab.
  • Resolve — sustain demanding attention for Resolve hours, then check each additional hour; failure normally causes Fatigued.
  • Presence — dependable personal allies as Connections, up to permanent Presence. The Non-Combat tab lists them.
  • Adaptability — a number of times per Adventure equal to Adaptability, reroll every die of one of your own Non-Combat checks (social checks and Perform Task included) and keep the new result. The sidebar counts the uses, a Non-Combat chat card offers the reroll while any remain, Reset Adventure Uses refreshes them, and Recovery does not.
  • Anima — at each Recovery, after every Resource regains 25% rounded up, distribute Anima extra points among Stamina, Focus and Mana.

Temporary Attribute changes never grant Skill Points, languages or Connections.

Click a Non-Combat Skill, Attribute or Key Aspect to roll it. Outside combat the pool is Attribute + Skill Rank (or Attribute + 5 for a Key Aspect). The GM sets a Difficulty from 1 to 10; your highest die must meet it. If the GM leaves it blank the roll posts open and the GM reads the highest die.

In combat, playing an Action or Reaction Card spends from a pool instead — your Action Dice on your own Turn, your Reaction Dice on everyone else's. You choose how many dice to commit (at least the card's minimum — never fewer than 2 — up to whatever's left in the pool); the sheet warns when you exceed the card's normal maximum of Attribute + Style Rank. When that maximum is below the minimum you still pay the minimum: the sheet rolls up to the maximum and burns the rest. Some costs are burned rather than rolled: Dash burns at least 2 (1 unit of Movement per die), Reconfigure and Stabilize burn 3, and a card's text can add a burned die. Burned dice never roll.

Commit first, roll when it resolves. During Combat the play prompt for an opposed card defaults to committing the dice and paying the costs now and rolling later: the chat card shows what was committed and a Roll now button. Declare responses, then press it when the chain resolves back to the card; targets are read at that moment and the prompt asks how many Success Dice the card needs. Cancelled marks the card cancelled with its dice and costs still spent. Untick the box to roll at once.

Your highest rolled die is your Success Die, compared against the target's Defense. When a check needs more than one Success Die, the prompt's Success Dice required field reserves that many highest dice, each of which must meet the number on its own. Every other rolled die that shows 6 or higher generates a Surge, which you spend on the options printed on the card; a reserved die never does. More dice means better odds and more Surges, but fewer dice left for whatever happens next.

Essence doesn't use a hit point bar. Apply Damage on the Core tab takes a hit as printed: up to three components, each with an amount and a Damage type, plus Breach or nonlethal flags and any flat reduction. Components resolve in order. Each first meets your Resistance or Vulnerability to that type, then your Resilience (a buffer that resets at the start of each of your Turns; Breach ignores it), then any Temporary Wounds, and only then fills a Core Wound space. You have 5 Core spaces, filled in order: 2 Light, 2 Serious, then 1 Critical. Each filled space attaches a Wound Card for the Damage type's domain (Physical, Mental or Spiritual) with its ongoing effect.

Your Wound State follows the highest-severity space filled. When the fifth space fills you are Dying: the Death Track advances at the start of each of your Turns, and acting while Dying pushes it once more per Round. Reaching the end is death, and death is final. Stabilize (a Basic Action, burn 3) stops the advance if its treatment requirements are met; a nonlethal hit that fills the track leaves you Stabilized and unconscious instead of Dying. Opening any Core space ends the incapacity.

Recovery

When the GM grants a Recovery, click Grant Recovery. Each Resource regains 25% of its maximum rounded up (halved and rounded up again while Fatigued), then Anima extra points go wherever you choose. The dialog lists your filled Core Wounds so you tick the ones whose Wound Card requirements were met: Light Wounds usually clear with care and one Recovery, Serious Wounds need post-Adventure Downtime, and a Critical Wound normally needs four weeks of appropriate Downtime care (twenty-eight qualifying days). Recovery also reduces the Death Track by 1 when you are not Dying, clears Psionic Strain, and removes 1 Manifestation Wound. It never restores Temporary Wounds, Temporary Influence, or Adaptability's Non-Combat rerolls.

Combat runs through Foundry's own Combat Tracker. When the GM starts an encounter, roll Initiative from your sheet or the tracker: commit from 1 die up to your base Action Pool. Those dice are rolled and totalled for turn order, and whatever you did not commit becomes extra Action Dice on your first Turn (ties break by the higher Success Die, then Grace).

At the start of your Turn the tracker clears your Reaction Pool, discards any prepared Action and its reserved dice, resets accumulated Damage, forms your Action Pool and applies Dazed's burn. Spend Action Dice on cards, Movement (burn 1 die per extra unit) and Basic Actions. Click End Turn to settle end-of-Turn steps (Gestalt upkeep, Combo) and convert whatever's left into your Reaction Pool: base pool plus unspent Action Dice.

Prepare Action (burn 2, then reserve dice) holds one Action for a trigger before your next Turn; the sheet shows a Fire button while it is held. A prepared Action or a Reaction uses your one response in a chain. Cards with a cooldown re-enable once per Round automatically, or once per Encounter when someone clicks New Encounter — ending one Combat in Foundry does not end the fictional Encounter.

Every Combat Style has its own thing to track, and the Combat tab shows the tracker for each Style you have:

  • Prowess — Combo pips (max 5, each +1 Movement) and a "dealt Damage this Turn" tick; End Turn drops 1 Combo when it is clear.
  • Ballistics — Establish Lock burns 1 Action die and records the target (two Locks with the Marksman Origin).
  • Gestalt — your Adaptation and its upkeep, paid automatically at End Turn or the Adaptation ends. Tick "assumed outside my Turn" to defer the first payment.
  • Cunning — Contingencies (one per Round, two with the Strategist), with a Trigger button; unused ones expire at your next Turn.
  • Magecraft — Threads: click a subtype to create one after its Action, hold up to 3 (duplicates allowed), consume from the list before a roll.
  • Psionics — Strain: the dice prompt offers 1 Strain for a free Surge; Vent burns 2 for 2; forced Strain past 6 becomes Breach Damage.
  • Leadership — Authority stored per card (two results per card for an Orator); click a result to spend it.
  • Ritualism — Rites with Trigger, Echo, Echo Limit and Possessed subject; three (four for an Invoker).
  • Calling — the shared five-space Manifestation Wound track and the header-menu entry into Full Manifestation. See the Full Manifestation Guide.

Everything that ends with the Encounter clears when a GM clicks New Encounter. See the Combat Styles Reference journal for each Style's full rules, Expertises and subtypes.

Play moves Planning → Adventure → Downtime → Planning. An Adventure ends when its central undertaking is resolved, abandoned, made impossible or transformed. Complete success is only one ending.

What an Adventure ending resets

Click New Adventure on your sheet once the table agrees the Adventure is over. It releases what is measured across the Adventure: Reach pressure, Adventure-limited Reach Triggers, and Uses that recover "at the end of the Adventure" (Augments and Equipment Cards whose own rule says so). Your Inventory allocation is released too, so you can choose a new Inventory the next time you reach your Armory. Temporary Influence from grants that have expired is removed.

An Adventure ending does not restore Stamina, Focus or Mana, heal Core Wounds, clear Core Influence, refill Consumable Kits, or repair lost equipment. Those follow Recovery, resupply and their own rules.

Downtime

Downtime has no fixed length and can hold one Recovery or several; the GM applies them. Critical Wounds count elapsed qualifying days of care during Downtime (four weeks by default). Retraining and Skill Tree purchases happen here as well. The Adventure's end also settles the Armory: keep what fits your Armory Limit, and sell, trade, return or discard the rest.
